opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that reinforcement learning only works when the model can actually get some reward signal. If you throw a model straight into extremely hard tasks, like very long-horizon reasoning problems or complex agentic tasks, almost every attempt fails. The reward is basically zero everywhere, so there's nothing to learn from. The gradient has no direction.

If you instead arrange tasks so the difficulty rises gradually, the model is always working near the edge of its current ability. It succeeds sometimes and fails sometimes, and that mix is where the most information is. Each success tells it something about what worked, and each failure is close enough to success to be meaningful. Then as its capability grows, you push the frontier a bit further.

It's quite similar to how people learn. You don't teach a child calculus before arithmetic. You build up skills that later tasks can reuse. For models, especially when we care about long chains of thought or many steps of tool use, the earlier, easier stages teach basic behaviors, like checking your own work, breaking a problem down, or recovering from a mistake. Those become the building blocks for harder problems.

There's also an efficiency argument. Compute is expensive, and rollouts on tasks that are hopelessly hard or trivially easy are mostly wasted. A curriculum that keeps difficulty matched to the model means more of your compute turns into learning.

And looking further ahead, I think this matters for scaling. If we want models to eventually solve problems that no human has a clean answer for, we can't rely only on human-written demonstrations. We need a path where the model climbs step by step, generating its own experience and getting stronger on slightly harder problems each time. Gradually increasing difficulty is one of the most natural ways to build that kind of self-improving loop.

r001.rationale: It says very hard tasks produce almost no reward signal and no useful learning direction, and that rollouts on hopelessly hard tasks waste compute.

r002.rationale: It describes deliberately arranging tasks into a gradual curriculum, but does not characterize reinforcement learning with a good sampling strategy as an implicit curriculum mechanism.

r003.rationale: It argues that models should not rely only on human-written demonstrations, but does not connect human-derived tasks or demonstrations to generalization problems.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core intuition is that reinforcement learning is fundamentally about getting a signal you can learn from, and if the task is too hard, you get nothing. If a model can almost never solve a problem, the reward is zero on nearly every attempt, and there is essentially no gradient to follow. The model is just flailing. On the other hand, if the task is too easy, every attempt succeeds, and again there is nothing to learn, because the model already knows how to do it. The useful signal lives in the middle, where the model succeeds sometimes and fails sometimes. That is where the contrast between good and bad trajectories actually teaches you something.

So the natural thing to do is to keep the model in that zone. You start with problems it can solve maybe a reasonable fraction of the time, it gets better, and then those problems become easy and stop being informative, so you move to harder ones. It is a bit like how people learn. You do not hand a first-year student an open research problem and ask them to figure it out. You give them exercises slightly beyond what they can currently do, and you ratchet up.

There is also a more practical reason. The long-horizon tasks we really care about, things that require many steps of reasoning or many actions in an environment, are very hard to reward directly. If you only give a signal at the very end of a long chain, the credit assignment problem is brutal. But if the model has already learned the shorter chains, the longer chain decomposes into pieces it is already competent at, and the learning problem becomes tractable. Difficulty progression is partly a way of smuggling in structure without having to hand-design dense rewards.

And I think the thing people underestimate is that this changes what you need from your data. You no longer need a fixed dataset that is uniformly hard. You need a distribution you can control, where you can measure the model's success rate and adjust. In some sense the curriculum becomes a product of the training process itself, because the model's current ability tells you what to feed it next. That feedback loop is what makes it feel like a scalable approach rather than a one-off trick.

r001.rationale: It says tasks that are too hard yield near-zero rewards on almost every attempt and essentially no gradient to learn from, explaining why such sampling is ineffective.

r002.rationale: It describes adjusting the task distribution to the model’s measured success rate and calls the resulting feedback-driven progression a curriculum produced by training.

r003.rationale: The human-learning analogy concerns task difficulty progression; the response does not identify human-designed tasks as a source of AI generalization problems.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that reinforcement learning needs a useful learning signal. If a task is too easy, the model already knows how to solve it, so there’s little to learn. But if it’s too difficult and the model never succeeds, it’s hard to discover which actions actually lead to a better outcome.

Gradually increasing difficulty lets you stay somewhere between those extremes. The model succeeds often enough to learn, while still having to develop new capabilities. As it improves, you can give it harder problems, and those new capabilities become the foundation for the next stage.

Of course, difficulty alone isn’t enough. The tasks need to teach skills that transfer, and the rewards need to reflect what we actually want. But if you can get those things right, a curriculum gives you a promising way to keep learning productive as the model becomes more capable.

r001.rationale: The response says overly difficult tasks may produce no successes, making it hard to identify useful actions. It does not communicate that sampling becomes too inefficient for effective learning.

r002.rationale: The response describes gradually increasing task difficulty as a curriculum, but does not characterize reinforcement learning with a good sampling strategy as an implicit curriculum mechanism.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention human-derived or human-designed tasks or link reliance on them to generalization problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that reinforcement learning needs a useful learning signal. If a task is too difficult, the model may try many times and never succeed. Then it gets very little information about which approach is better. But if the task is too easy, solving it again doesn’t teach the model much.

So you want tasks near the boundary of what the model can currently do—challenging, but with some chance of success. As the model improves, you increase the difficulty. That gives it a way to build capabilities step by step, instead of expecting it to discover a very complex solution all at once.

The difficult part is making that process work automatically: how do you generate the right next task, and how do you verify that the model actually solved it? If you can do both reliably, you have a promising mechanism for continued improvement.

r001.rationale: It says overly difficult tasks may require many unsuccessful attempts, yielding little information about which approach works.

r002.rationale: It describes raising task difficulty as the model improves, creating a step-by-step learning process—an implicit curriculum driven by task selection.

r003.rationale: It does not mention reliance on human-designed tasks or any resulting generalization problems.
